metadata.note:
Passenger rail at Phoenix, Arizona, 1887-1996 - a gap in this dataset until 2026-08-26, when the map carried the Southern Pacific Sunset Route past Maricopa but nothing into Phoenix itself. Three corridors are covered. (1) The Maricopa & Phoenix Railroad, whose first train on July 4 1887 gave Phoenix its first rail connection, running 35 mi southeast to the Sunset Route at Phoenix Junction (now Maricopa); it passed to the Arizona Eastern in 1910 and to Southern Pacific in 1924, and its passenger service ended in 1933. (2) The Santa Fe, Prescott and Phoenix Railway - the Peavine - opened to Prescott in 1893 and through to Phoenix on March 13 1895, giving the city a northern outlet to the Santa Fe transcontinental main at Ash Fork; merged into the Santa Fe in 1911, cut to the single daily Hassayampa Flyer in 1955, realigned around Prescott in 1962, and ended in April 1969. (3) Southern Pacific's 1926 Wellton cutoff, which put Phoenix on a transcontinental main line and carried the Golden State and the Sunset Limited until Amtrak rerouted the Sunset via Maricopa in 1996.

The Phoenix, Tempe & Mesa Railway's 1895 Mesa Branch, Tempe east to Mesa, is drawn too, under the same three owners as the main line; its geometry is largely approximate - see its geometry_quality. The Peavine is drawn as three connected pieces (Ash Fork-Prescott, Prescott-Skull Valley, Skull Valley-Phoenix) plus the 1962 Prescott bypass as a fourth. That split exists so the drawn years stay honest: the 1962 line change replaced only the Prescott portion, so the Prescott pieces stop in 1962 while the Skull Valley-Phoenix piece runs on to 1969. Features are likewise split at each ownership change, per Rule 4, with identical geometry reused across the successive owners.
metadata.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap, fetched 2026-08-26. Route relations 14865112 (Arizona Eastern Railroad Phoenix Division), 9099462 (Tempe Industrial Lead), 9097925 (UP Phoenix Subdivision), 9118814 (Wellton Branch, disused) and 1453787 (BNSF Phoenix Subdivision), pulled whole from the OSM API and chained by shared node ids; plus an Overpass bbox dump of railway=abandoned ways tagged old_railway_operator=AT&SF between Ash Fork and Skull Valley for the original Peavine alignment. Douglas-Peucker simplified at 25 m. Every straight-line bridge over 0.4 km is named in the relevant feature's geometry_quality.
metadata.mileage_check: Ash Fork-Prescott 60.6 mi (documented ~58-60), Prescott-Skull Valley 22.4 mi (documented 23 mi over Ramsgate Hill), Skull Valley-Phoenix 112.6 mi, giving 195.6 mi Ash Fork-Phoenix against a documented ~195 mi. Maricopa-Phoenix 35.5 mi against ~35. Wellton Junction-Phoenix 133.9 mi against a documented 137. 1962 bypass 66.2 mi against the 82.7 mi it replaced. Mesa Branch 5.25 mi against a documented ~5 mi.
not_yet_sourced: The Mesa Branch's alignment east of Rural Road in Tempe is a straight-line chord, not a survey. Abandoned Rails describes remnants 'along 8th Street in Tempe' and says the western portion, where it meets the UP secondary main, was rehabilitated for Valley Metro light rail - but the light rail runs on Apache Boulevard at about 33.4148, roughly 500 m south of the disused fragment at 33.4196-33.4211 this file traces. Which of the two the branch actually used west of Rural Road has not been resolved.

The exact 1895 opening date of the Mesa Branch is not sourced; Abandoned Rails gives only 1894-95 construction. The 1895 start year drawn here is the construction end, not a documented first-train date.

Between Ash Fork and Paulden, OSM carries two roughly parallel alignments: an abandoned one to the west (tagged old_railway_operator=AT&SF) and today's BNSF line to the east. The pre-1962 features draw the abandoned western one, assuming it is the original 1893 alignment, but no source has been checked to confirm that the eastern one is a later relocation rather than the original.

The Phoenix-Picacho leg of the Southern Pacific Phoenix Line is drawn on the current Union Pacific alignment. OSM relation 14865111 records a 14.4 mi alignment in use 1924-1935 east of Chandler that differs; the 1926-1935 years are therefore drawn on later track.
Every headway_min in this file is an estimate. No employee or public timetable was consulted for any segment.
The 1933 end of Maricopa branch passenger service is taken from the Wikipedia article, which does not cite it.

The Phoenix & Eastern / Arizona Eastern lines east and south of Phoenix (toward Florence and Winkelman, roughly 100 mi of branches the Santa Fe, Prescott and Phoenix article also mentions) are not drawn.
Valley Metro Rail (light rail, Phoenix-Tempe-Mesa, opened December 2008) is not in this file and is not yet anywhere in data/.

amtrak.geojson's 'Amtrak: Sunset Limited' feature draws 1971-2026 on the post-1996 Maricopa alignment. Its geometry should be split at Wellton Junction and Picacho Junction so the 1971-1996 years use the Phoenix routing drawn here; until then both alignments show for those years.

metadata.rule_notes: Rule 1: nothing here is drawn past the end of its passenger service - the Maricopa branch stops at 1933 though freight ran on and part of it survives as UP's Tempe Industrial Lead; the Peavine stops at 1969 though BNSF still works the line; the Wellton cutoff stops at 1996. Rule 4: the Maricopa & Phoenix (#8D9F00), the Arizona Eastern (#4527A0) and the Santa Fe, Prescott and Phoenix (#1B5E20) are new to this dataset and took new colors; Southern Pacific (#C1272D), Santa Fe (#003DA5) and Amtrak (#1c4e80) reuse the colors already established in southern_pacific_sunset_route.geojson, atchison_topeka_santa_fe.geojson and amtrak.geojson. The Santa Fe, Prescott and Phoenix is given its own color rather than the Santa Fe's because it was an independent company running its own trains until the 1911 merger.

properties.speed_source: estimated: a ~35 mi branch worked by mixed and local trains over unballasted desert track subject to Gila and Salt River washouts; no timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM, 35.5 mi against a route documented at roughly 35 mi Maricopa-Phoenix. Assembled from OSM relation 14865112 (Arizona Eastern Railroad Phoenix Division, railway=abandoned) for Maricopa-Kyrene, relation 9099462 (Tempe Industrial Lead) for Kyrene-Tempe, and the Tempe-Phoenix portion of relation 9097925 (UP Phoenix Subdivision). One straight-line bridge of 1.70 km at Kyrene where the abandoned grade and the surviving lead are not connected in OSM; two further bridges under 0.1 km. The Tempe-Phoenix leg is drawn on the CURRENT alignment into Phoenix Union Station (1923); the 1887 M&P entered Phoenix at its own depot and the exact original approach and Salt River crossing are not drawn.

segments.note: First train into the Salt River Valley ran July 4 1887, giving Phoenix its first rail connection - to the Southern Pacific Sunset Route at Phoenix Junction, now the town of Maricopa. Routed east through Tempe and Mesa rather than west of the South Mountains after those towns lobbied for it. Flooding on the Gila and Salt regularly cut the line, at times stranding passengers at one end for a week. Daily-each-way service assumed, not sourced.
sources: Segment-level: opening date and routing from the Wikipedia article and Abandoned Rails; the headway is an unsourced assumption.

segments.note: Consolidated December 1895 with the Phoenix, Tempe & Mesa Railway as the Maricopa & Phoenix & Salt River Valley Railroad - a renaming of the same operation, so it is drawn here as one company rather than split. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: December 1895 consolidation with the Phoenix, Tempe & Mesa per Abandoned Rails; headway unsourced.

properties.speed_source: estimated; carried over from the Maricopa & Phoenix era, no timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: Same traced geometry as the Maricopa & Phoenix feature - see its geometry_quality. Split out as its own feature under Rule 4 because the Arizona Eastern, not the M&P, ran the trains in these years.

segments.note: The Maricopa & Phoenix & Salt River Valley was absorbed into the Arizona Eastern Railway in 1910. The branch remained Phoenix's only link to the Southern Pacific transcontinental main until the Wellton cutoff opened in 1926. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1910 absorption into the Arizona Eastern per Wikipedia; headway unsourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Same traced geometry as the Maricopa & Phoenix feature - see its geometry_quality.

segments.note: The Arizona Eastern became part of Southern Pacific itself in 1924. Passenger service over the Maricopa branch ended in 1933, by which time the 1926 Wellton cutoff had made the branch redundant for through travel; the southern section was abandoned in 1935 and the northern end survives as Union Pacific's Tempe Industrial Lead. Drawn years stop at the end of passenger service, per Rule 1.
sources: Segment-level: 1924 Southern Pacific absorption, 1933 end of passenger service and 1935 abandonment of the southern section all from the Wikipedia article (the surviving-lead claim there is uncited).

segments.note: Chartered May 27 1891, construction south from Ash Fork began August 17 1892, and the line was operating to Prescott by April 1893 - two years before it reached Phoenix, which is why this stretch is drawn from 1893 while the rest of the route starts in 1895. Frequency estimated.

segments.note: In 1955 the Santa Fe cut Peavine passenger service to a single daily train each way, the Hassayampa Flyer, connecting at Ash Fork with the Chicago-California main-line trains. properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM relation 1453787 (BNSF Phoenix Subdivision), sliced between Ash Fork and Skull Valley - 66.2 mi against the 82.7 mi of original alignment it replaced. No straight-line bridging. This is the post-1962 alignment and is drawn only for post-1962 years.

segments.note: New line completed April 21 1962: leaving the old route about a mile and a half east of Abra, west across Chino Valley at Paulden, then south down Williamson Valley Wash, Long Canyon Wash and Tonto Wash to rejoin the old line at Skull Valley - bypassing Prescott entirely. The Hassayampa Flyer used it for its last seven years; the final regular passenger service to Ash Fork ended in April 1969 when train 42 was discontinued. Frequency estimated at one train each way daily.
sources: Segment-level: the routing and the April 21 1962 completion from the Sharlot Hall Museum article; the April 1969 discontinuation of train 42, the Hassayampa Flyer, from the Wikipedia article.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM, 209.2 mi total: Wellton Junction-Phoenix comes to 133.9 mi against a documented 137 mi, and Phoenix-Picacho Junction to 75.3 mi. Assembled from relation 9118814 (Wellton Branch, disused), two surviving rail chains and one abandoned link at the Wellton Junction end, and both halves of relation 9097925 (UP Phoenix Subdivision). Four straight-line bridges, the longest 1.42 km. CAVEAT: the Phoenix-Picacho leg is drawn on the current Union Pacific alignment. OSM relation 14865111 records a 14.4 mi alignment in use 1924-1935 east of Chandler that differs from it, so the earliest years of this feature are drawn on later track. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 4 ruled segments totalling 64 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: Southern Pacific completed the north cutoff - the Wellton cutoff, or Phoenix West Line - in 1926 specifically so that the Golden State and the Sunset Limited could run through Phoenix instead of connecting at Maricopa. 137 mi of single track with a few sidings between Phoenix Union Station and Wellton Junction. This put Phoenix on a transcontinental main line for the first time; the Maricopa branch's passenger service ended seven years later. Frequency estimated from two through trains each way.
sources: Segment-level: 1926 completion, the stated purpose of routing the Golden State and Sunset Limited through Phoenix, and the 137 mi Phoenix-Wellton Junction figure all from the RailPAC account of the Wellton Branch; headway unsourced.

segments.note: Amtrak took over the Sunset Limited in 1971 and kept it on the Phoenix routing until 1996, when it was rerouted away from Phoenix in favour of Maricopa - Southern Pacific, absorbed by Union Pacific that same year, wanted out of a line with deteriorating track and very light freight traffic. About 64 mi of the cutoff, from east of Roll to west of Arlington, has been out of service since. This is why Phoenix, the largest US city without intercity passenger rail, disappears from the map in 1996. Headway estimated on the train's long-standing tri-weekly frequency; the exact frequency in each year is not sourced. OVERLAP: amtrak.geojson's own 'Amtrak: Sunset Limited' feature already spans 1971-2026 on the current GTFS shape, which crosses Arizona via Maricopa, so for 1971-1996 the map draws both alignments and only this one is correct for those years; that feature has been given a geometry_quality note saying so.
sources: Segment-level: the 1996 reroute away from Phoenix in favour of Maricopa, the SP/UP motive and the 64 mi out of service since 1996 from the RailPAC account; 1971 Amtrak takeover from the Sunset Limited article. The tri-weekly headway is an unsourced assumption.

properties.geometry_quality: APPROXIMATE - 5.25 mi drawn against a branch documented at roughly 5 mi Tempe-Mesa (the 1933 ICC abandonment covered 5.14 mi of it: 0.623 mi at Tempe plus 4.517 mi Creamery-Mesa). The right of way is almost entirely gone and OSM holds only stubs of it, so only 0.79 km of this line is traced from real rail - a railway=disused fragment running east from Rural Road in Tempe at about 33.4211,-111.9261. The rest is straight-line: a 1.66 km western leg from that fragment back to the junction with the Maricopa & Phoenix main line at Tempe, and a 6.01 km eastern leg from the fragment to the North Mesa depot site at about 33.4127,-111.8536, fixed by the abandoned Phoenix & Eastern spur that reached the shared station. Both legs are chords between known points along the fragment's own bearing; the real branch may have jogged with the section-line grid. The junction point sits exactly on this file's drawn Maricopa & Phoenix main line. Do not read the eastern 3.7 mi as a surveyed alignment.

segments.note: Built 1894-95 by the Phoenix, Tempe & Mesa Railway to reach Mesa from the Maricopa & Phoenix main line at Tempe. The two were consolidated in December 1895 as the Maricopa & Phoenix & Salt River Valley Railroad, so the branch is drawn under the same company and color as the main line rather than split out for the few months the PT&M stood alone. Abandoned Rails treats the PT&M as a name the Maricopa & Phoenix operation carried at the time. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: 1894-95 construction and the December 1895 consolidation from Abandoned Rails; the PT&M index page confirms the branch as Tempe-Mesa and lists M&P, PT&M, SP and UP as its successive operators. Headway unsourced.

segments.note: Southern Pacific from 1924. Passenger service ended in 1933; 1930 aerial photography already shows the branch used only for storing rolling stock, with industry surviving at the ends - the Creamery siding to the east and sidings around the North Mesa depot. The abandonment application (ICC docket 10079, filed 17 July 1933) covered 0.623 mi at Tempe and 4.517 mi between Creamery and Mesa. Drawn years stop at the end of passenger service, per Rule 1; the middle stretch survived as freight-only trackage known as the Creamery Branch and is not drawn.
